transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-18 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Dana Li (ForgeWorks Head of ML), Miguel Ortiz (Platform), Sana Rahman (SecOps)
Shared links: Redwood POC benchmark template - https://redwood.internal/poc-benchmark-template (redwood link), ForgeWorks sample dataset location - s3://forgeworks-test/poc-samples (not shared in recording)

Summary:
- Objective: scope a short POC for capacity sizing and autoscale guardrails; determine reserved GPU baseline, burst strategy, and fallback behavior if reserved capacity is saturated.
- Success criteria discussed: p95 latency target, cost per 1k tokens, and stability under traffic spikes.
- Benchmarks: plan to run three phases: baseline throughput, spike injection, and fallback validation.
- Timeline: kickoff infra checklist this week, benchmark run next week, 2-week POC window thereafter.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Okay, um, hi everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on this — we have Priya, our solutions engineer, on the call to map out the POC sizing and autoscale guardrails. Dana, do you want to do a quick intro?
[00:14] Dana: Yeah hi, uh, thanks Alex. I'm Dana, head of ML at ForgeWorks. We're evaluating inference platforms to replace our homegrown sharded model serving; primary goal is to reduce operational overhead and stabilize tail latency. Miguel will cover infra details and Sana's on sec.
[00:28] Miguel: Yep, hi all. Our stack is mostly k8s on EKS right now, some services in GCP, and we use HashiCorp for secrets.
[00:36] Priya: Great, quick note — we often propose a reserved GPU baseline for POCs to make burst/fallback testing deterministic. That gives you predictable throughput and then a burst layer on top — either cloud burst or Redwood-hosted spare capacity.
[00:50] Sana: Quick question about data — for POC we'll use synthetic masked examples, nothing with PHI. Also we need KMS integration for any private routing.
[00:58] Alex: Got it. So the key things to scope: expected concurrency, token generation patterns, acceptable latency SLOs, what success looks like for ForgeWorks, and whether you want the POC in Redwood Hosted or Private VPC.
[01:12] Dana: We're leaning private VPC as a hard requirement for production, but for the POC we're open to hosted if it speeds up onboarding. We need to validate KMS/HSM behavior though.
[01:24] Priya: Understood — we can run the POC with a Private control plane and customer VPC peering; that validates KMS integration and audit logs. It adds a small setup window though — typically 3–5 business days for peering and firewall rules.
[01:38] Miguel: That fits. Our network team can make a slot Thursday for peering.

[05:02] Alex: Let's dig into workload sizing. Dana, what are your current peak and baseline numbers? Even ballpark helps.
[05:12] Dana: Sure, our nightly scoring job is heavy — roughly 120M tokens per hour at peak batch jobs, but online requests are the harder case: p95 tokens per request is around 1.2k, p99 spikes hit around 4k tokens; concurrent online requests currently average 120 concurrent sessions with spikes to about 700 during feature releases.
[05:36] Priya: Okay, that p99 at 4k tokens is important. For serving we need to understand whether you stream tokens or prefer full-response batching; streaming keeps tail latency tighter but changes batching strategy.
[05:50] Dana: We stream to the client. Also want to preserve partial responses if fallback occurs.
[06:00] Priya: Good note. For baseline reserved sizing we usually pick a configuration that covers sustained 90–95% of load within SLO and then rely on burst capacity for short lived spikes; that keeps cost predictable. For models, what are you planning to run — Llama variants, or a smaller proprietary model?
[06:16] Dana: We'll be testing an open 34B and a quantized 13B for most online inference. The 34B is for higher-fidelity paths but we prefer to failover to 13B if latency or cost constraints demand it.
[06:30] Alex: So fallback policy could be: if p95 latency exceeds X or queueing grows beyond Y, route to the quantized 13B variant or enable reduced context/shorter generation.

[09:45] Miguel: On infrastructure, the biggest unknown is how Redwood's reserved pools map onto our VPC peering. If we do Private, will traffic flow directly or through a NAT? We need to keep egress minimal for compliance.
[09:58] Priya: With Private we support VPC peering that keeps traffic internal — we can avoid public egress. We'll need your CIDR ranges and firewall egress rules.
[10:09] Sana: Also audit logs — we need request-level logs with token counts stored for 90 days, plus cryptographic proof of key usage. Does Redwood expose those?
[10:19] Alex: Yes, Redwood can stream audit logs to your S3/GCS bucket and we integrate with KMS for envelope encryption. We'll include the exact retention and format in the SOW.

[14:02] Dana: Success criteria from my perspective — first is functional parity: responses match our current model qualitatively for a set of 200 eval prompts; second is latency: p95 < 350ms for 13B under baseline, and p95 < 900ms for 34B under baseline; third is cost envelope — we want a rolling estimate for $ per 1k tokens under baseline and under 3x spike.
[14:30] Priya: Those are good targets. For the POC we can set experimental guardrails: baseline reserved GPUs to meet 95% of regular traffic, then run controlled spike injections (synthetic traffic) to exercise burst for 30–90 seconds and measure fallback correctness.
[14:48] Alex: We'll also capture metrics: request queuing, token/sec, GPU utilization, batch size distribution, and cold-start latency if we spin nodes.

[18:20] Miguel: About burst: do we have two paths — a Redwood-hosted burst pool and cloud on-demand expansion? What failsafe if both are saturated?
[18:32] Priya: Yes, two-tier burst is typical: first Redwood spare pool (fastest), then cloud on-demand nodes (slower to ramp, costlier). Fallback strategies are layered: 1) route to quantized or smaller model; 2) truncate generation length; 3) degrade to synchronous shorter mode or return cached answers; 4) degrade non-critical features. We recommend a sequence of fallbacks with clear thresholds.
[18:56] Dana: We like the idea of a deterministic fallback sequence rather than ad-hoc. Can the POC test all of those?
[19:04] Priya: Yes — POC phases include a fallback validation where we intentionally saturate the reserved pool and verify routing decisions and correctness of partially served outputs. We'll also test graceful degradation for streaming clients.

[22:10] Alex: On SLAs during POC — we guarantee the experiment configuration will be deterministic, but production SLAs are a separate commercial conversation. For POC we provide runbook-level guarantees and commit to reproducing benchmark runs for a second pass.
[22:28] Miguel: We might want logs to show token-level billing so finance can project costs.
[22:34] Alex: We'll export a cost report per test run showing tokens, model variant, and GPU-hours — that will be in the benchmark spreadsheet.

[26:50] Priya: Quick note on caching: prefix caching might reduce repeated tokens for your use case — if you have long shared prompts we can cache KV state across requests to lower GPU load. Is that something you use?
[27:00] Dana: Yes, we use shared system prompts for context; caching could reduce token generation by 10–30% depending on overlap. We'll include an example prompt corpus in the dataset.

[30:15] Miguel: For the reserved baseline number, do you have a rule-of-thumb mapping from concurrent sessions and tokens/request to GPUs?
[30:24] Priya: Rule-of-thumb: for 13B quantized on A100-like hardware, assume ~60–80 tokens/sec per GPU under streaming and moderate batching; for 34B it's closer to 20–30 tokens/sec. But it's workload dependent — sequence length and batchability change that. For your numbers (avg 120 concurrent, p95 1.2k tokens) rough back-of-envelope: 13B baseline might need 6–8 GPUs reserved to cover steady load within SLO, 34B would be much larger. We'll formalize with microbenchmarks.
[30:55] Alex: We'll provide two sizing options: conservative (cover p99 expected sustained) and efficient (cover p90 sustained + burst). Which do you prefer for the POC?
[31:05] Dana: Efficient is fine for the POC as long as we test the p99 scenarios in the spike phase.

[34:40] Priya: Benchmark plan (high level): Phase 0: environment setup and VPC peering; Phase 1: baseline throughput with real-ish traffic at 70% traffic; Phase 2: spike injections (3x and 5x sustained for 60–90s); Phase 3: fallback validation and correctness checks against 200 eval prompts plus 500 synthetic streaming requests. We'll collect token latencies, GPU util, queue depth.
[35:05] Dana: Sounds good. For correctness we need human validation on a subset — we'll review 50 examples post-run.
[35:12] Alex: We'll include a link to the evaluation sheet in the SOW and request a small team to review.

[38:50] Miguel: Timeline concerns — the Private VPC peering and KMS proofs add time. If peering is Thursday, when can the benchmark run start?
[39:00] Priya: If peering completes Thursday and we get firewall rules and creds same day, bench can start Monday. So earliest end-to-end is about 3 business days for setup, then 2 weeks for the POC window.
[39:12] Alex: Proposed calendar: infra checklist Friday 2027-05-21, peering slot Thu 2027-05-20, bench exec start Mon 2027-05-24, POC window 2027-05-24 to 2027-06-07.
[39:25] Dana: That fits our release cadence.

[43:20] Sana: Security asks — can you confirm you will not persist raw request bodies in logs, only metadata and token counts? Also need proof of key usage for KMS.
[43:30] Alex: Yes, we can redact request bodies; audit will include request IDs, token counts, model variant, and cryptographic key usage metadata. We'll attach the SOC2/ISO extract and KMS integration checklist.

[46:10] Priya: Edge case: what if both Redwood pool and cloud on-demand are saturated and you still have a large incoming spike? Our recommended rate-limiting approach is to apply a controlled admission policy that returns a graceful 429 with a small hint payload linking to a retry timeline, and for streaming we can send a terminal partial answer. We'll test that behavior in phase 3.
[46:30] Miguel: Good — we prefer predictable failures over silent queueing.

[49:05] Dana: Any notes on instrumentation — we want Grafana dashboards and traces.
[49:11] Priya: We'll provide a dashboard template with token metrics, queue depth, GPU utility, batch sizes, and request histograms; and a tracing hook to join with your Jaeger tracing.

[50:40] Alex: Okay to recap and next steps: Alex will send SOW and two sizing options; Priya will send benchmark plan and scripts; Miguel will share traffic and CIDR info; Sana will send compliance checklist. We'll schedule infra call for 2027-05-21.
[51:02] Dana: Thanks all, excited to get started.
[51:10] Alex: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the documents.

End of transcript.

Notes on artifacts:
- SOW template and benchmark spreadsheet to be attached in follow-up (Alex).
- Priya to run a lightweight microbenchmark on 13B quantized and share latency per token numbers before full POC.
